With the half price stickers, buying two was easy, even with the cost of parking thrown in. The stop at Green Eggs Cafe may have been a little over the top, but added to the quality afternoon.

Gold Garden is a middle of the road Chinese/American shop in the Homestead Plaza II, in Columbus, NJ.  It has 5 tables for those choosing to eat in.  The front of the house is a large counter where the wife of this H & W team holds court with efficiency and a smile.  The menu is what you would expect.    My Sesame Chicken was served on a plate (rather than in Styrofoam), with Fried/White/Brown rice options, as well as soup or soda.  At $5.65 it was one of the better prices I have seen for this luncheon combo.  Taste-wise, it was okay, with a nice pile of chicken breaded, fried, and smothered in semi-sweet goo.  You know ... the way you have seen it a million times.  Plenty of rice made earlier in the day.    The plaza where it is located also has ice cream and cupcake stores right next door, for those seeking things from all the nutritious food groups.  Luckily, the cupcake shop is closed Monday and Tuesday.    Temptation is everywhere.

This is the second OwowCow I have customered.   It is housed in a former industrial space and the reuse is attractive, if rather basic.  Small public space with a few tables, and the expectation that most people will take their ice cream and leave.   Their flavors are exotic-sounding, and for the most part they succeed in producing the subtle tastes that are seldom found in ice cream parlors.  My "Regular" sized cup of Indonesian Vanilla and Banana Caramel was smooth, creamy and required some attention to appreciate the variations and their mixture on the tongue.   The sizes are smaller than the competition, and the prices a bit higher, at $5. for two small scoops of whatever flavors you choose. That may be a good thing, as it does suggest slowing down to enjoy the moment over piling on luscious calories.   The shop is across the parking lot from Big Bear Natural Foods, and people have been known to park there without hassle.

The Peter J. Camiel Travel Plaza is a smaller scale rest stop along the Pa turnpike.  While all the plazas are being redesigned and modernized for the new century, this one, while clean and efficient, and provisioned with the expected vendors from Starbucks to Roy Rogers and the ever-present Wawa like shop, this one lacks the comfort of the others on a busy day.  The lines tend to knot with each other.    Still, it generally does what is supposed to do; provide plumbing and victuals for the road weary traveler, and help them on their way to their ultimate destinations.    It is functional and an improvement over its predecessor.  Who was Peter J. Camiel?  A Philly politician of the Rizzo era who was prosecuted for corruption in office, convicted, and ultimately vindicated on appeal to the higher courts. As his legacy he had this rest stop named after him.

On a recent return visit I sampled their cronut and macaroons.   Both were pretty good.  Sweet, but not overly so.  Textured well, so that the pleasure came from a combination of senses.   While still not close to a Boulangerie Parisienne, at least it is a reasonable facsimile of one, especially for those with sweet teeth, who have never been to Paris.

While I'm not a Starbucks guy (too often burnt beans), this new drive thru sit down plant in the Village @ Newtown Shopping Center is very cool. Laid back, smaller footprint, friendly accommodating baristas, and decent breakfast profile, make for a pleasant interlude. Panoramic view of the ever expanding choices coming online in this primary commercial zone in Newtown. Can see Melt Shop, Factory Donuts, Naked Chocolate, Oishi, Nothing Bundt Cakes from my small deuce in the window.   Here for a quick Saturday morning meeting, I enjoyed their oatmeal with blueberries, crannies, raisins and a touch of brown sugar (How come you dance so good?!). Perhaps, a little too much packaging for a health planet, but they do have choices. Even the Pike's Roast was more flavorful and less bitter than usual.   Meeting went well, so this $$$bucks could become a strong house for getting together in private conversation. There is enough ambient noise from the polished concrete floor, high metal ceiling and sound system to mask any but the loudest voice.

Apparently the sibling of 1st Oriental Supermarket on 6th Street in South Philly, with similar layout and the same products from live fish through Vietnamese noodles and Thai sauces. Yeah, it has an odor of over ripe fruit and spilled frog water, but that goes with the territory. While some find it offensive, it reminds me of the outdoor markets throughout Asia where the smells are part of the experience.   We had the good fortune of eating dim sum next door at China Gourmet before shopping. It was very good and a great opening act for the aisle cruising to come. Made for a complete excursion to the East.

Zhang's China House has apparently been sold and under new ownership for several years already, but the new information has not been loaded onto Yelp until today.   Never made it to Zhang's, but at least it had a website with menu and a little history. The new folks don't know how useful it is for marketing to be on line here and present themselves to the most active restaurant people in the area.   Hope giving them a Yelp page helps.

I read the few reviews while waiting for my Turkey and Swiss Hoagie to be served in the back room dining area. I admit to feeling some restaurant remorse imagining what I was about to get with a Snapple for my $9. (hair sandwich with attitude played in my head).   Instead, I received a very decent fresh soft Hoagie roll stuffed with my selections, including copious hot and sweet peppers, and a nice smile and "enjoy your lunch," from my server. I enjoyed the sandwich, and put the trepidation to rest. Nothing wrong with the meal. I am not in downtown Trenton that often these days, but I would certainly consider adding City Deli Hoagie Shop to the list of alternatives along Willow Street.

It may not have the shelf space of the large Asian Markets in Flushing, nor the mystique of my favorite subterranean shop in Philly, but H Mart is only ten minutes from home and provides me with most of the Asian specialties I would otherwise get stuck on the Verrazano Bridge to reach, or be forced to pay ten bucks to park in Center City.    Returned last night to pick up Chinese Eggplant, Ginger Root, Assorted Frozen Dumplings, Hot Dumpling Sauce, Crispy Chili in Oil, and a big can of Wasabi Sweet Peas (Thailand), for meals and snacks over the next few weeks; while checking out the fresh fish, and other exotics, like an anthropologist enjoying a stroll through a museum.    I have yet to take a seat in the little café to taste what's going on there, but until I do, the rest of the store suits my needs perfectly.

Liv & Charlie Real Food on North Union Street, Lambertville, NJ, is a morning/afternoon shop serving healthy and tasty meals on treadle tabletops in this beautiful river city. The people are friendly and confident in the quality of their menu.  I stopped in last week for breakfast and totally enjoyed the experience. Their french toast made with fresh challah was excellent. The egg/vanilla/sugar/cinnamon mix soaked in well and the hot grill caramelized the edges just right. Most important, the house used pure maple syrup and cold butter to allow me to doctor the slices the way I like best. I sipped my strong coffee (with fresh whole milk) as the beurre melted and the syrup eddied and swirled on the plate.   It was delicious. I kept cutting the toast into smaller pieces to maximize absorbency and stretch out the pleasure.   It was a quiet morning with only one other table occupied. The music track was alternative rock that suited the atmosphere of the house.   Liv & Charlie know what they are doing.   5 Stars all the way!

We had a great La Villa Traditional Square Pizza here last week. I had forgotten how delicious their pies were. It was loaded with peppers, onions, mushrooms and sausage, and baked to a wonderful crispy crust(see photo). Service was also friendly and prompt. The black clad servers certainly kept a certain 21 year old family member entertained.   However, the app special Crab Cake was drenched in a cheesy white sauce that overwhelmed the titular star of the show to such an extent that the crabbiness of the crustacean was lost.  The big Greek Salad while plentiful lacked imagination and an impressive dressing.  I would not ask for either of those again.   But, in the end it is all about the pie.  La Villa's are vastly superior to any of its nearby competitors, and can stand their own with some of the best across the river in Jersey or Philly.   Happily, it is much closer in Morrisville, in a nicely appointed renovated Pizza Hut structure in the middle of a strip mall parking field off Pennsylvania Avenue.

I now know the downside of having a pizza parlor make pies for display purposes.  If you are unfortunate enough to come in for a late pizza slice lunch, you end up eating old pizza from the display, rather than anything remotely fresh.    I learned this lesson the hard way a few days ago, when I stopped in after 2:30 for a small repast to tide me over until dinner.  My Tomato Pie was sauce without cheese (In my world it is sauce over cheese). It was okay, but basically too acidic from sitting around for many hours.  Too, the plain slice while large, had an overworked crust that proved tough and chewy rather than crisp as a cracker.  Time had not been kind to it.  I liked the gentleman who prepared my slices in the oven and brought them to the table, and it was not his responsibility to make a new pie for me.  Still, there outta be a rule that says display pizzas are dumped after being out in the open for more than 2 or 3 hours, so they are not reheated beyond human tolerances.

A mall is a mall is a mall.  While this is closest to home, I generally find malls to be sterile barns.  But, for the associated AMC theaters across the parking fields, a few restaurants in the circle around it, and many medical offices, I would likely never frequent the place.   It seems that malls are a 20th Century phenomenon whose time may have passed them by, unless they are reconceptualized and reconfigured to meet the more dynamic needs of families, and consumers.  A sense of community purpose is required that is both traditional and state of the art.   Until that happens most malls will continue to lose stores and visitors. Just as the horse and buggy were replaced by the automobile, and the urban core was redistributed to the burbs (and now contracting again), the mall will eventually evolve into a new kind of commercial center than includes everything the old village maintained, but wired into today.

As large government bureaucracies go, the local office of the Social Security Administration on Lincoln Highway (Rt. 1), Fairless Hills, Pa., is doing a pretty good job.    The appointment given my client to deal with a question of overpayment was easily secured over the phone, and when we arrived at the given hour, our wait was no more than 15 minutes.  That is fairly precise for an agency that deals with all sorts of issues and people in varying degrees of stress and ability to communicate.    The representative who met with us was professional and knowledgeable about what we were there to discuss.  We quickly reached the heart of the matter, reviewed the facts and alternative resolutions, and decided on the best course going forward.    Everyone was satisfied with the quality of the meeting, as well as its efficiency.  We left the building in under 45 minutes from when we entered.    It is difficult to rate government from a "fan" or "Woohoo" perspective as needed for higher ranking, but in this instance, the "A-Okay," is from the heart.

Perhaps the most beautiful urban park in the USA, Fairmount captures both the historic grandeur of Philadelphia, as well as its awesome potential. And, of all the great buildings and events that have taken place there, the one most strategically placed and incredibly majestic vista is seen when standing on the Belmont Plateau overlooking Center City.   While living in the neighborhoods near the Art Museum (Brown St.), West Philly (UPenn) and in West Center City (25th & Delancey), I was always close enough to walk, bike or drive to the Plateau for a softball game, holiday picnic or sleigh ride in the snow. It remains my favorite single spot in the City to relax, breathe deep and capture the essence of what makes this town great.   Sure, it's the people, but looking down into its urban core gives a sense of human potential and unique possibilities.   In short, the view is inspirational.

Excellent bagel joint in Doylestown Borough. Small customer area, with room in back for ovens, preparation, storage and display case. The rounders have a crisp biting crust, while the inside has enough air pockets to keep it fairly light enough to allow the flavor of the topping (roast onion flakes) or whatever is added in the prep(butter & Swiss) to come through strongly.   I appreciate the bagel baker who knows not to knead the dough too long, which hardens the bread and makes it too dense. Too, here they are boiled and then baked in the right proportion to create the optimal bagel.   Having La Colombe and Ellis Coffee in house is also a big plus, as they are both top shelf Philadelphia roasters that have found success nationally and internationally.   These Borough guys are not fooling around. They give their customers quality bagels and first class java for a fair price. It wouldn't surprise me if their success was assured and they grew their enterprise as far as they wanted to take it.

This Chick Fil A wannabe does a decent job of frying chicken strips into a reasonably good signature sandwich.  Fresh chicken, crisp breading, and not overly oily.    The fries are average, and the corn is sweet.   As good a choice as any if you find yourself needing sustenance while at Oxford Valley Mall.

Reading through the more recent reviews of the Continental Tavern I had the impression that while most people liked the atmospherics, they were less enthused with the cuisine. While the two of us only had their "Best of Bucks" burgers, fries and soft drinks, we departed thinking we have had better elsewhere.

This is another of those Yelp doubles, that have more than one entry for the same business.  The other, Original Dominick's Pizza Shoppe, has a few more reviews.  The confusion lies in the addresses.  The number on the front door is 1045, the address for the "Pizza Shoppe" page.  1067 is given as the address for ODP, but that number is not on the door.    Until that is straightened out, just check out both pages for a full display of reviews, tips and photos.   Mange bien!

When I walked in my first reaction was, "Wow! This looks way different than Cosi. Very colorful, light and airy, and lots of smiling faces behind the counter."    I had the Chicken Salad Pita Sandwich with a side of Grilled White Beans, which was really a thick bean soup.  Everything was fresh, if not totally original or outstanding in composition and taste.  It was very satisfying, and warrants a return visit to check out more items on the menu.  The manager came over to chat with us.  She was warm and engaging, and explained that part of the Zoes corporate culture was to contribute to the community.  She asked us to think of them when we needed donations of food for a good cause.  It seemed that it was too busy a place for meetings in a quiet corner, but the offer was well received here.   Zoes seems to be a very positive addition to Newtown's Sycamore Street core, and with the many alternative food outlets right there, it will help draw more people to the area when they are looking for a good meal in a great location.   Good luck, Zoe.

Poppy's Pizzeria sits alone on a desolate stretch of Woods Lane, Langhorne, Pa. I didn't even know it was there for a dozen years until a detour took me past it recently.   It was Friday night - Pizza Night - so,what the heck?!  The layout was casual with three sections in the dining area. Tight booths and tables all around. HDTVs mounted high in the corners. We seated ourselves. Our server arrived quickly and introduced herself with menus in hand. We ordered a round pie half mushrooms, half sausage; a dozen Buffalo wings and cheesesteak calzone.   Everything was okay. The wings were hot from the hot sauce bath, but arrived looking overdone with several bones exposed and charred, but tasty. The pie had the right ingredients, if less than a full complement of shrooms and meat and lacking a crisp crust. The calzones was stuffed to the gills with steak, but could have used more onion and pepper within for added flavor. Took most of that home.   Poppy's has promise, and with a more skilled hand in the kitchen could find themselves in a more elevated zone.

One of my regular stops while in Tucson for the gem and stone extravaganza in late January every year is Miss Saigon (Yes. I've seen the play). It is another of the North Campbell Avenue string of pearl restaurants that I found and stuck with over many years.    The shop is comfortably designed with a relaxed Asian décor.  The staff is warm and usually prompt in that offhand attentive way we all know.  The menu is simple and everything I have tried has been solidly satisfying.    My choices tend to be the same each year, as I obviously can't get there often.  An order of Spring Rolls (Shrimp, Pork, Greens, Noodles in translucent Rice Paper), Mixed Wok Veggies with Tofu in Ginger Sauce, and one of several great Pho alternatives. My young son, as always the genuine food critic, came to love their Chicken Wings, Orange Chicken, and eventually, the Pho Ga. All these dishes have been enjoyable and strong enough to induce some loyalty.    Yes. I have eaten equally good Vietnamese cuisine elsewhere in the USA, but it is great to know I don't have to give anything away when I want some in Tucson.

This was my third visit in so many months, and this time I ordered the Eggplant Parm Grinder (finished with a visit to the over to plasmatize everything).  It was great.  Thin sliced, sautéed, Eggplant, chunky Tomato Sauce, and fresh tasting Mozza on a large Italian Loaf; all brought to a sizzling climax with a brief visit to the pizza oven before serving.  For totally satisfying and delicious lunches, Tina gets 5 BIG ONES!

Rosa's is tucked away in a tiny 4 store strip center just off North Campbell, and very easy to miss. But, it is worth finding.    The family run enterprise is a staple of Tucson, dishing out very good South of the Border plates at reasonable prices.  It is one of those few shops I always return to when in town for the gem show extravaganza in late January/early February.  There is usually a short wait for a table, as the space is small and a tight squeeze.    The food is decent, if not haute cuisine, and quite tasty and filling. A couple of margaritas or cervesas after a long day looking at hot rocks is the best way to begin the chill down.  The service can be erratic, but they make up for it with attitude and good humor.    One of the best things they have is a wall full of calendars for purchase with classic Mexican art the prime selling attraction.  I love hanging one on my office wall as a recollection of my time in Tucson, and Rosa's colorful hospitality.

I have been here numerous times for meetings, but only spent the night here once.    The front desk is always efficient and friendly.  The staff working the meeting rooms know what they are doing.  The lounge areas is surprisingly comfortable at night if you don't want to spend all night in your room.  The rooms are adequate with most expected conveniences. Never had a problem with cleanliness or noise.  Comfortable beds and pillows.  Plenty of hot water.    The location just off Rt.95 is both good and bad.  It is easy to find, but not close to any services like restaurants.  You will need your vehicle to go into downtown Newtown or Yardley, but both are worth seeing and have plenty of good food options. A little further away are Trenton and Princeton.  A drive through Bucks County is always pleasant if you have the time.  Upriver are New Hope and Lambertville; both great stops for art and antique hunters.     It is certainly a viable reasonable alternative for travelers of all stripes.

The County Theater appears to be the only cinema in Bucks to show independent and limited distribution films.  For that it has my appreciation.  I certainly wish the Newtown Theater, the oldest in the country, had the same policy.  The digital projection is a big plus.   I was there last Sunday for a 4:00 pm show, and it was packed. Not an empty seat in the house! Applause to the members and others who take interest in this institution, as it makes it a  fine community resource.   If there is any downside (and I hesitate to mention it), it is that when crowded, the seats are a bit cramped, and not as comfortable as the "big house" theaters. Too, sometimes you get some attitude from the regulars who have their favorite seats, and refuse to move over to make room for another couple, forcing them to sit apart. Not much the theater can do about that.   Over all, a wonderful piece of Bucks cultural heritage alive and well today.

Hard to beat a decent breakfast at half price.   I found their French Toast to be above average, although their coffee needs some work.    Still, when I can walk out of a restaurant after only paying 3 and a half bucks for a full plate and java, I am a happy man.   Saw a table card that said something about Tuesdays being "AYCE" Burger Days.    Very tempting.

While the price of gasoline in Newtown seems to be higher than anywhere else in the surrounding area, the quality of the mechanics is also higher.   Steele's Gulf is a very good option should your car need repair.  They are fast, reliable, and have integrity with their work.

What can you say about the complete, in your face, sweet, gooey, dripping down your chin, jelly donut experience?  Great, right? If you go for that, and fresh hot glazed burn your tongue goodness, then this is the place for you, and everyone else with a sweet tooth. Forget the diet. Go get some!!!  PS.  Personal fave - glazed raspberry jelly filled. I see the light!

Steele's Gulf and Steele Rick Service Station are the same place. Yelp should combine them.  This is an honest repair shop, with a family that has an excellent reputation for reliability and good communication with its customers.

The addiction has not improved, and if anything it has gotten worse.   Turns out, KK has a fundraising plan that allows the purchase of a larger quantity of their sinfully outrageous donuts to non-profits doing fundraising for their organizations at a nice discount. I guess that helps salve the gluttonous conscience when participating with your church or scout troops, but ordering most of the donuts for yourself.  The thought of someone else eating your donuts is just too much to bear.    May as well man-up and accept the fact that the crack they put in the donut fillings and glaze is overwhelming you, and that a stint in an in-patient addiction center is the only way to deal with this monster habit.    A hot cup of coffee to help wash them down is a solid second option.
See. RITE AID PHARMACY @ this location for reviews.
There are two entries for this establishment for some reason.   Be sure to check them both to catch all the reviews.

Wawa, the roadside rest stop version, named after the famous village in Pennsylvania of that name, has it all figured out.    Give people choice.  In coffee, sandwiches, snacks.  And, they will come.  Make all things reasonably good and competitively priced, and they will become loyal.    The newest shops take their cues from 21st Century design.  Large, airy, clean, with gasoline out front, and bathroom in the back. People like this feel and will find their way to them.  Just like Sheetz, Rutters, and major road service areas, they provide a more satisfying experience then the older, smaller, mini shop version of the late 20th C.   They don't offer the variety of a Starbucks or other national chain vendors, but their proprietary issue is decent, and saves a whole lot of shekels.   I can't say that I am a fan, but the concept and experience is growing on me.

Second Street Bagels is under new management and working hard to up the quality of the rounders exiting their backroom oven. From my first bite this late September morning it seems they are succeeding.   I was fortunate enough to ask the owner where the bagels were made, and he was happy to take me on an impromptu tour of the operation. I followed him behind the counter and through the kitchen door. The large boiling pot was full of brine and the rack was full of aluminum trays with bagels just out of their bath and chilling before going into the oven for finishing. I knew that the boil helped set the crust's consistency, and that lye or sugar/molasses water were traditionally the elixir of choice, but didn't know that brine was an option.   It certainly worked to produce a excellent bagel. Thin crust. Nice bite. Pleasant mildly salty malty dense texture within. With sweet butter and nutty Swiss slices, it was an enjoyable bagel. Decent java, too.   Wish Second Street Bagels well with its new ownership team.

Most, if not all, TJ Maxx stores are the same.  Same layout. Same labels.  Same prices.  Same long wait at check out.    While I don't shop here for a fashion statement, they do provide a fair assortment of the basic necessities of haberdashery - primarily, dress shirts, socks and other garments that come packaged in multiples, at steep discounts off the MRP.  (Right, that is why they are also known as, "unmentionables.")  So, this warehouse appears to be smaller than others in the region, but the inventory seemed about the same.  If you have patience, and enjoy the sport of bargain hunting, this could be one of your stake out safaris.   Word of caution. Don't trust the sizes/prices posted on the store-attached tags.  They are often wrong.  Always check the garment directly to save the hassle of getting the wrong size and being forced to make returns.  After all, TJ Maxx is about saving money; not your convenience, nor fashion sense.   Caveat emptor!

Golden One is a new Chinese American kitchen just behind Neshaminy Mall in the same center as DMV. It is a large room with well spaced tables and a fast takeaway operation. The menu is extensive and they do have a sushi guy slicing and wrapping seaweed.   My first impression was positive for a simple Egg Foo Young plate with Egg Roll, Wonton Soup and white rice. The base stock for the soup was chicken broth that was not too salty and had decent wonton/dumplings that were not thick skinned, nor with questionable meat filling. The egg roll was even better with adequate roast pork mixed with cabbage and a few greens. The EFY was two pancakes filled with more pork and veggies and a better than average brown sauce that seems to have been prepared just in time.   Overall, I liked this meal on their Combination menu for dinner. I particularly appreciated the absence of obligatory broccoli florets, which is way overdone by most Chinese restaurants.   The house being clean with friendly service was also a pleasant positive touch.   Yes. I grade these places on a curve.

I am not certain how many names this tiny end of strip Chinese house uses to attract attention, but, I drove by yesterday looking for Little Basil and found the awning in front of their shop was still shown as, "Levittown Kitchen." It had another name before that, but ownership may have changed. No doubt, however, that both listings are active on Yelp, despite the fact that they seem to be paying for advertising as Little Basil only.   Not that this approach to advertising changes anything about their cuisine. It is the same two table China house offering Thai options in addition to the traditional Sino/American fare. I liked their general's chicken and egg roll lunch deal. Better than some; not as good as others. Their sauce seemed to have been freshly made and not as heavily goopy as most.   I am interested to know whether using different names for their restaurant actually is good for either business. Can't fault them for trying something unusual.

Found in the Fareway Market on Germantown Avenue, Chestnut Hill, Poppy's Cafe is a cubbyhole of a shop dealing in good coffee and a few sweet cookie and sliced pound cake to keep their cash register ringing up sales.   The multigenerational family running the business is friendly and knowledgeable about their products, and seem to enjoy spreading their information to those customers who ask.   I chowed on a fresh chunk of vanilla iced pounder, washed down by a medium roast java lightened with milk. Very pleasant combo for the drive home.

The oldest movie theater in the USA, and a registered historic landmark and non-profit, the Newtown Theatre is a community treasure, playing current movies in an environment that brings you to the 1950's.   The physical layout is as old as this suggests, with a tiny ticket booth and refreshment area that would fit in your closet.  Climb the narrow stairs to the balcony, and feel what it was like when your grandparents and great grandparents went on dates, and could only be alone in the dark with a chaperone between them. A great old place, well worth the trip.   PS. Check their website to see a photo in the snow in the New York Times. www.newtowntheatre.com.

I remember the uproar when Applebees and another fast food shop were permitted to enter Newtown.  It was the beginning of the end to life as we knew it!   Not.  Applebees has taken its place as a well utilized restaurant in the Village of Newtown Shopping Center.  It follows the national formula and does not deviate beyond the mean.  It is busy for lunch, dinner and late night, and fits the need for a modestly priced option among all the high end restos in the area.    I don't go often, but I am glad it is there.  When I do, I stick with the ample fresh salads, and an occasional burger.  I sit at the bar when I dine alone, or one of the booths when with family.  I have not had a bad experience, nor ever felt it was misplaced here.    Go. Enjoy. Have a good time. This shop is locally owned by The Rose Group, and even if you prefer to avoid chains that expropriate your money out of the community, this particular franchise does not.  You can have a clear conscience.

Seamless transition from Tea Talk to Tea Chat as the new ownership takes control.  Same friendly, attractive staff.  Same drinks and snacks.    This seems a good place to get your Boba On!  My Hot Green Bubble Tea tonight was nice company on the road back to Bucks.    Would certainly visit again, and perhaps discover what the story is with these pearls being sucked through oversized straws.

BBQ Chicken PA is a Korean Fried chicken stall in the Assi Market, Welsh Road, North Wales. It is in the small food court on the right side of the warehouse-sized store. I was looking for a late lunch of double deep fried wings, plus some to take home to the family.   I thought I ordered enough with Secret Spicy sauce, but turned out the order taker put in the order for half my request, despite my double checking with him. That bleach job must have turned his brains blond in addition to his hair. Yet, maybe he was doing me a favor.  Eating the first one let me know that these guys were not the super crisp wings I've had elsewhere. Nope. These were slathered in the garnet red goop with good flavor, but the skin was not crunchy as anticipated. Plenty of meat in the bone, but lacking the corresponding bite.   Suddenly, the dude's inattentiveness was a small blessing as it cut my disappointment in half. Ten okay wings were better than twenty less than optimal pieces.   I'll be sure to thank him next time I'm in the neighborhood.

I have seldom been at a big city airport that I enjoyed, so I have no need for harshness. For international flights I only use it when it is the cheapest of the alternatives by a substantial amount.  Terminal D (United) is no better or worse than others I have been forced to use.  Never expecting to have an airport experience any better than barely tolerable, Philly meets my expectations.   I will say that I just had the best shoeshine there. No brushes. Just soft damp rag and good wax.  Hope it lasts for a few weeks in China.

This BK sits out on Nottingham Way next to China Express, part of the new commercial zone being developed at the old fairgrounds site. It is designed for drive around service, with a dangerous nod to in house dining. To walk in requires crossing the drive through lanes where most drivers aren't paying attention to pedestrians.   The drive up ordering system needs help because it is difficult for driver and ordertaker to understand each other. I could not hear what the young guy was saying to me, but it was apparent he didn't hear me well either. I repeated myself three or four times and hoped for the best. I was pleasantly surprised that I received what I asked for.   I ate at my desk. The breakfast croissant sandwich was small, but decent. The coffee just mediocre. Prices were very close to what is available at the many delis, cafes and morning taverns in the area, so unless time is at a premium, I prefer the other alternatives for higher quality and comfort.   Searching for a word to capture the experience, "uninspired," seems about right.

The bagels were denser than I like, but otherwise Redhouse Bagels is a busy place on a rainy Saturday morning. Bakery in back, plenty of friendlies working the front of the house, and around ten tables for a sit down quick bite breakfast. My Onion Bagel, butter and Swiss sandwich was tasty with lots of baked onion flakes falling off with each bite. It was fine.  No, the turnoff came all at once when I took a visit to the men's room. There was a leak in the sink faucet that was causing black mold to grow at the base of the spigot and on the strainer over the drain. It looked like the condition had been active for a while. Given how toxic black mold is to some people it was shocking that it was allowed to remain without active professional intervention.   Please take care of this before someone becomes ill from it. If the Department of Health sees it, the shop will be shut down until it is returned to a safe condition.

Made a return visit after an hiatus of almost 2 years, and was pleasantly surprised to find the house redecorated with more comfortable seating and brighter lights.   Accompanied by a teenager and his mom, I again realized that American fast burgers are very popular.  I tried one of their discount double burgers and fries, and found that while they were no match for Five Guys or that ilk, they were still decent and satisfying.  Watching the young guy wolf down his Double Baconator was eye opening. He was totally into it.  Oh, and the fries was ample and crispy.    Time for an upgrade.   No apologies!

This Mario & Franks in Fieldsboro, NJ, is much smaller than number 4 in Trenton, but is nicely finished with a small, but comfy dining room.  Service is fine and prices on lunch specials are downright inexpensive.    So, when I saw a Chicken Parm Sandwich with Fries and Drink for $6.99, I was tempted.  Unfortunately, the excitement turned to disappointment once I dug in to the huge plate that was served.  Biggest hot sandwich I had seen in a long while.  At least a foot long, cut in half, and a pile of taters that took up the other half of the large square platter.   To my tongue, the chicken fillets had been frozen and deep fried, rather than pan sautéed, which is the right and tasty way to cook it.  Maybe cheaper to use frozen chicken and fry alongside the potatoes in a vat of common oil, but it sure kills the expectation that comes with ordering any parm dish.  Really did not taste good.   This was a shortcut to Never Never Land.

The Pineville Tavern is worth a try just for the historic structure and ambiance in the older rooms.  Someone once said you can't eat the atmosphere, but here it is possible to almost taste it.  The institution is worthy of respect. The latest changes have been both good and bad.  Read the other reviews to understand the complaints and disappointments. For me, this place has always been about beer, wings, burgers, and rice puddling.  The other stuff designed to attract a wider audience may not float everyone's boat.   Stick with what they do best, and you will leave happy and full.

Not the best bagel experience in the area, and not the worst.   The store is spacious enough for a number of tables and a long line waiting for service. Bins full of rounders appear smaller than my last Manhattan visit a few years ago (Clearly not real Manhattan Island bagels that are often larger than a saucer in diameter.) Still, my onion, butter and swiss had decent texture, loads of onion flakes and a good bite. Their coffee could stand a better bean roaster and more choices.   Service suffered from understaffing. There was one woman taking orders and working the griddle, making for a hectic burnout shift for her, and growing queue. When the owner/manager came out from the back, and put on plastic gloves, things got better, but he was not well trained in food prep, so the butter spread was uneven, and only a single slice of cheese was placed within - where a minimum of two is the normal allocation, and often more. Too, the transection did not completely separate the halves, so when one side was lifted, the other tagged along and fell apart.   I attributed that to having a bad morning.
An extra star for their community involvement is warranted.  Boy Scout Pancake Breakfast was a fundraising success.

Cheesesteak Review -  Dino's is primarily a take out pizza joint on Street Road in Warrington, PA. We wanted to eat while the food was prime, and opted to mange at one of the three tables in the front of the house. Son and I were in the mood for steak sandwiches, although the pizza looked appealing.   This Saturday night they had a three person operation in the kitchen, with Dino on the grill. The room was a bit chilly on an early December night, even with the little space heater. Still, hunger and strong aroma of the beef being chopped and tossed by the chef overcame any temporary discomfort.    The sandwiches were excellent. Fresh crusty rolls, huge load of grilled beef made in house and sliced just before touching hot steel to guarantee juiciness and surprisingly good flavor. A work of culinary art.   We congratulated Dino for hitting the cheesesteak sweet spot, and assured him we would return. Never too far to go for a great Philly steak sammy. And, if the pizza is as good, the beginning of a long delicious relationship.

INCOMPLETE  I have stopped at Priori's on three occasions when their sign says they are open for business over the past few months, and each time the shop was locked up tight without notice nor explanation. I even called while parked in front of the building, without answer.   This is a recommendation that you call before you go, so you don't waste time like I did.   Wishing them the best, whatever is going on.

This Asian grocery, butcher, fishmonger, green grocer has been open right off Roosevelt Blvd @ St. Vincent Street for several years, having purchased the former 1st NE International Market in 2015. It is very similar to the supermarket at 6th and Washington in South Philly. It has just about everything you need for the complete Chinese kitchen, including pigs feet to fat green frogs, and dozens of vinegars and soy sauces for any dish imaginable.   True, the odor of fish on ice and tanks full of lobster and talapia can be pungent, but that is part of the experience and brings me back to the street markets all across Southeast Asia.   If you need it, they likely have it. If they don't have it, think twice whether it is really necessary.   Even found those Japanese versions of KitKat Bars in strawberry and green tea flavors!

The old stable is now populated by diners enjoying the bucolic, high beamed ceiling, stone floors and exposed kitchen.  If outdoor dining in nice weather is your thing, you can be easily accommodated next to the boccie court and outdoor bar.   It seems I am there most often for special community events, and the layout works well for isolating small groups in places that do not overly interfere with the regular dinner patrons.  The food is family style Italian, meaning if there are more than 3 of you, many of the dishes come piled high and placed centrally on the table where everyone can partake.   The food has always been solid, both meats, fowl and pasta.  The service is much better than average, with black and whites hustling around to be sure everyone is getting what they expect in a timely and friendly, while professional manner.  The last event buffet consisted of Chicken Francaise, Vodka Rigatoni, Eggplant Rolatini, Grilled Veggies, Italian Bread.  All worth the price of admission.    Sure glad someone thinks enough of their guests to schedule a social/political event in such pleasant surroundings.

For fast food franchised joints, Chick-fil-A does a very good breakfast sandwich.    My Sausage, Egg and Cheese Biscuit was far better than their equivalents at McD's or Burger K.  It is larger, fresher, tastier, and the biscuits themselves flakier and more buttery.    This was a drive thru order at this newish outlet.  They made a small mistake in my favor by throwing in a box of Taters at the bottom of the bag.  I didn't order them, but neither was I charged.  I wasn't aware of it until I arrived at my destination and saw what was in the bag.    Nice to come out on the high side of the transaction.  So often, these deals break the other way.

Actually in Wrightstown at 5 Points on Rt. 413.   Primarily a take out place, but there are a few tables if eating the food piping hot out of the kitchen is important (it should be).   The food is standard Americanized Chinese food. There must be one cookbook they all work out of, or a convention they all attend to get the same items on every menu around the continent. Still, Panda Garden is on the higher end of the quality spectrum even if the output is fairly much the ubiquitous fare we all know. I have had the Wonton Soup who's broth is above average; the various Chicken and Sauces, which are solid, but uninspired and sometimes overcooked; and the Noodle dishes and Foo Youngs, which are also acceptable. Just nothing to write home about unless you are having a very boring day and feel homesick.   If you find yourself in this part of Bucks County this choice is as good as you are going to find. It is an A - Okay option.

This Target is a great example of the old fashioned true department store, with a little of everything you need for daily existence.  Clothing, food, lighting, kitchenware, electronics, sports equipment, music, and automotive - all under one roof.  It may not have everything you want, but it generally has everything you need.    Heard that it is a good place to work, especially compared to the other Big Brother Big Box stores.    Not the highest quality, but not the lowest, either.    Even the snack/coffee area is offered as a convenience to their customers.    If you remember EJ Korvettes and other last century highway superstores, Target will make you feel a little nostalgic.

One door closes and another opens...Such is the Circle of Life.  Giovanni's Custom Tailoring has opened in the space formerly occupied by its predecessor, Frank DeRito Men's Clothier.  Dino continues to tailor expertly and bring his warm, cosmopolitan charm and gifted abilities to the same location where he has worked for more than a decade.    I recently ordered a suit (S. Cohen of Montreal) and had Dino make the necessary fine tuning adjustments for my long arms and legs.  All done at a very reasonable price.  He is truly a master of the needle and thread, and knows before I do what will look good on me.    Hopefully, Giovanni's will carry the same quality clothing as Frank DeRito, and will likewise have the great sales when exceptional suits, jackets, coats, sweaters, shirts and ties can be purchased at prices not normally associated with high end Newtown.   At least, I can pray that happens.

When Lynn's was open, and Leo was scooping out wisdom along with his personally roasted coffee beans, this shop had to be one of the best places in the region to pick up a bag of beans after discussing you tastes with the Man. It was from Leo I discovered Tanzanian Teaberry, and some of his own mystical blends.   Sadly, the storefront is now closed.  But, all is not lost.  The Grapevine on North State Street, just one block away now has Lynn's coffee for sale with many of the most popular varieties still in large burlap bags for sampling.  Chuck, the owner of Grapevine is more than happy to fill your order.  While his book of knowledge is quite different than Leo's, he has more than his share of great tales to tell.    By all means, buy your coffee here, and while you're at it, pick up some organic veggies, and your nutritional supplement needs.  Very cool store if you can find the front door behind the wall of hanging potted plants surrounding it.

While most of the bakery sweets are heavy, their icing is wonderful.  I have sampled many of their buns, cookies, bars, cakes, and they are all fun to eat.  My favorites are the Apple Cake which reminds me of the densely moist version my Yiddish grandmother made on most holidays, and the Lemon Bars which are equal parts tart and sweet with powdered sugar dusted on top, and a firm crunchy base.    Both are addicting and require self control to make them last.

Strictly take out with $10. minimum for credit card purchase.    The menu is extensive, both Chinese and Sushi, and the prices reflect the absence of tables and service expenses.  The front of the menu has a nice statement about healthy eating being their goal, and that the food is all natural, low calorie and how it is the, "only specialty take out serving authentic Chinese & Japanese in this area."   Maybe, but what they do not claim is that it is tasty or high quality cuisine.  Sadly, speaking only of the Chinese side of the menu, it is not.  The ingredients may have integrity, but the resultant dishes are ordinary and lacking in most redeeming qualities other than being filling. The food isn't bad, it just isn't very good.    I wouldn't attempt to compare it with the food produced in New York or Philly, but even by the rather pedestrian suburban standard, Lotus Garden hardly measures up to its peers.    It may offer gluten free dishes, but by the same token, it also offers tasteless ones.   Best to keep looking for a more satisfying fast Asian meal.

No doubt the Trenton Pork Roll Festival could have been something special given the concept and all the vendors and bands that showed up. However, the word is that 2,000 people invited themselves for a 300 person party, and the logistics were just not capable of handling the scene.  Too, a massive thunderstorm in mid afternoon blew out the electricity, shutting down the bands, and dousing everyone and their pork roll sandwiches. The canopies were not able to control the deluge.    I was there for a few minutes in early evening after the last of the heavy downpour, but not post the straggling showers that seemed to hang over Trenton Social all day.  After standing in line and getting soaked, I decided discretion was the better part of valor, and beat a retreat to find a dry place for dinner.    Please try again next year, fellas.  You are on to something here.

The Bagel Zone? Is that a veiled reference to The Twilight Zone?  I ask only because on a recent early morning visit there on my way to court in Mt. Holly, there were a group of men gathered there at pushed together tables that seemed like they were from another planet.  Men In Black kind of thing. They dispersed soon after I sat down with my bagel and coffee and opted to face them rather than the window behind me. Guess they didn't like the scrutiny.   Anyway, this was my first visit there, and although the staff was friendly and the prices rock bottom, the primary product was only average.  My Onion Bagel was richly sprinkled with Onion Flakes, but the texture of the bagel was more the consistency of dinner roll rather than a thick skin encasing a chewy but air-pocketed inner body. It was fresh and completely edible, but lacked the "bagelessence" I sought.   Coffee was decent, and with change from a Lincoln, the price was certainly right.

Shady Brook Farm has been an institution in the community for decades.  From a small farmers' market it has grown organically into a multifaceted event driven destination.  The family always comes up with new ideas to entertain on a grand scale. Our favorites are the Autumn Corn Field Maze, Pumpkin picking, and the Christmas Lights Night Drive.  All are done on a scale that let's you know it is not quite professionally polished, but done by the owners'/farmers' own hands.    Sadly, a large part of the Farm will cease to exist in the next year to become a medical facilities center.  The pumpkin field will be no more.    Be sure to visit Shady Brook Farm several times over the coming seasons, as the good times and culturally bucolic experiences will soon pass into history.

While BB&B offers almost everything you could possibly need in an American bathroom, bedroom or kitchen (other than large appliances), there is definitely a human scale problem.  With 30 foot ceilings and housewares stacked to that peak, walking through the narrow isles gives a sense of claustrophobia and strained neck.  Everyone is funneled through the counterclockwise flow of the warehouse, with side trips down tributaries to find the particular thing you need.    This feeling of being overwhelmed by the canyons and islands makes for an unpleasant experience.  It is true that the "one stop" nature of the store has benefits, and that the ability to examine multiple towel options, or alternate coffee making technologies, is educational.  Yet, the sheer verticality of the space is ever-present and unpleasant. Compare to Home Depot with similar floor to near- ceiling merchandise. There, the aisles are wider and there is a better proportional scale. There is no feeling that a towel slide could wipe you out.  Maybe their next gen factories will be more appealing.

Two Slice & Coke Review  I was hunting for a missed dinner nosh to spare me those overnight hunger pangs, and Fat Tony's appeared on my Yelp radar. Not many reviews, but you know what they say about 'any port in a storm'.   Fat T's sits in a small commercial strip right next to an excellent new member of the Morrisville restaurant community. Big window permitted full view of the house with only two deuces on the floor. Clearly a take out operation. But, I like my pizza well done and right out of the oven, so I sat down to await my first bite of Tonypie.   It wasn't what I hoped.   Although well done was requested, what I got were two slices without firm chassis that refused to lift off the paper plate when I elevated their crusty end. Saggy and limp. I had to pick up the laggard points and throw them over the thick end, making them more pizza roll, than pizza pie.   The sauce had promise, but if my slices can't salute when called to attention, they can't serve in my tomato pie army.

After a second stop in for a few more slices to find out if Gabriel's pies were as good as first impressions, I am very happy to report that they are even better than remembered!   Our Italian Sweet sausage and Fresh Mushroom reheaters were requested well done, and that super heated scorched bottom was just perfect. Rigid chassis. High point. Great crunching bite. Balanced sweet/salty sauce. Quality sausage and white thick slices shrooms.   Loved it so much I thought I was across the Delaware River in Jersey.   Gabriel come blow your horn.

Nice country store feel for locally sourced ice cream studio.  Super friendly and informative people.  When I asked the difference between the Vanillas - Madagascar, Tahitian, and another exotic island label, I was told that the most "vanilla"-flavor was the Madagascar version, while the others were either too light in flavor or more of a marshmallow sentiment.  Went African Isle with a scoop of Blueberry Lemon.   Creamy texture, full blown taste bud involvement.   Instant smiles and satisfaction.    Clearly, a labor of love expressed in imaginative combinations and high quality execution, wrapped up in a easy to miss village ambiance shop.    The road sign is too small, so unless you know it's there, or have visited Carousel Gardens for other reasons, very easy to miss.    Worth finding.  NOTE 8.28.2013 - This ice cream just won a 10 Best In USA award from the Huffington Post.  Congratulations!

It has been too long since I visited Barbie's for one of their exquisite pretzel dogs - all beef garlicy homemade weiner topped with jalapeño, sauteed onion and American cheese - all wrapped up in one of their freshly doughed, twisted, salted and baked pretzel skins.   Eat'em while they're hot for peak actualization.   Today their drink special was a Pumpkin Latte Shake. A good, cool, sweet gourdy slush that epitomizes Halloween. The small 6 ounce cup was $4.25, including a free hand twister.   Pennsylvania Dutch comfort food par excellence.

It may be true what the other Yelpers say about the quality of the breakfasts here, but as I was here for lunch I can't comment on the morning sustenance.   I can say that this looks to be a fairly recently renovated Jersey diner, very clean, friendly, and broadly diverse menu.  I sat at the small counter next to the hostess/manager as she was being mentored by the owner about ordering from purveyors.  He was calm, articulate, and seemed to appreciate his people.  Impressive.  Of course, the fact that he was dealing with a gorgeous employee may have had something to do with it.    My lunch was ordinary.  The Chicken Salad on Rye Toast was just okay.  The toasting seemed to have taken the life out of the bread, as it was overly dry and brittle.  The Chicken Salad was ample, but lacked much flavor.  The cup of Chicken Noodle Soup was a nice touch, but too salty.    Given the positive vibe of the place, I would certainly return for breakfast, but lunch, not so much.
Definitely time for an upgrade! I have become a fan. 4 Stars with a bullet.

The Fresh Works is a small family run chain of sandwich shops in and around Bucks County, specializing in cheesesteaks, wraps, burgers, and traditional deli fare. This shop in the Richboro Shopping Center has some new competition from the Super Wawa that opened up right up the street.  I wish them luck where they go head to head in the sammy department, but they do have the edge in seating, comfort and roots in the community.  The mini tuna hoagie (5") I had for lunch yesterday was decent.  Plenty of tuna, lettuce and tomato in a very good house baked torpedo roll.  Actually, the bread was the best part and worth return visits. The sandwich was served open face with tomato slices on top. It was a lot of lunch for $5, with added swiss.  Definitely, value there.   Reviews mention the steak sandwiches as being praiseworthy, but as a faithful devotee of Steve's Prince of Steaks, I may not discover what I might be missing. Still, it is good to have a solid choice in Richboro that does not require skipping a local business in favor of a large franchise.

After a second stop in for a few more slices to find out if Gabriel's pies were as good as first impressions, I am very happy to report that they are even better than remembered!   Our Italian Sweet sausage and Fresh Mushroom reheaters were requested well done, and that super heated scorched bottom was just perfect. Rigid chassis. High point. Great crunching bite. Balanced sweet/salty sauce. Quality sausage and white thick slices shrooms.   Loved it so much I thought I was in Jersey.   Gabriel come blow your horn.

Great reuse of a 19th Century firehouse in the heart of Norristown, now a museum and distillery for premium vodka, whiskey, gin, and special batches of other unique blends. Three story open barroom where once horse drawn firewagons were housed, with upper floor sleeping room for those once on duty and a rear space full of stainless steel distilling tanks and vats. Fascinating place I wish I had time to explore with a knowledgeable guide.  Maybe next time, but tonight we were there for a political fundraiser for a local county official seeking reelection. Judging by his choice of party venue, the open bar and the look of everyone present to support him and wish him success, he has a strong chance of re-election. Even the local congressman was there to wish him well.  With speeches and a good buffet (and that open bar) there was opportunity for limited sipping and light dining in the midst of the very loud din of conversation  between the soapboxing. The distillery itself remained background to an excellent soiree.   Will definitely return for more tasting and a tour.

This fairly new freestanding Dunkin' Donuts in the wilds of Eastampton, NJ, was empty when I arrived for a post court late breakfast and java. In my recent experience, the proliferation of DDs has diluted the quality and consistency of the signature products, so that the coffee is often harsh and undrinkable in some shops, and still quite good in others.  Same thing for donuts. Some have good ones. Some don't.  As everyone is trained the same way, it comes down to water quality and cultural familiarity with sweet rounders.  This joint was pretty good.  There was a small communications problem, but what I ultimately received (breakfast sandwich and joltin' joe) were both hot and tasty.    No complaints.  And, a nice facility with a large lounge area for those who want to get some work done, or take a comfortable nap - perhaps, both.

Oh, Danny Boy....  Why so unassuming?  Why hidden in a forlorn strip of 20th Century retail excess?    Why aren't you sharing your gift with the entire Tomato Pie craving world?   The lights. The lights are calling...!  Your T. Pie is among the best I have sampled in my pizza-loving life.  It is in the local pantheon of greatness occupied only by a few other mozzarella souls - DeLo's, JoJo's, Ivy Tavern, Joey's, and a few others in the Mecca of the Pizza Universe, Brooklyn.   Micro thin crust firm enough to hold the topside without a quiver.  Sauce, chunky and mildly sweet with a hint of basil. Cheese hidden beneath with a gentle saltiness to balance the smiling acidity above.  Not a single drop of oil on the aluminum tray despite a spritz of pressed olive applied as the final touch before reaching the oven.  And, the sweet Italian sausage, home grown, and crumbled around the disk amply, with a wonderful aroma and fresh textured taste.    Though you labor in obscurity, Danny, your artistry is not lost on those who treasure the magic only a steamy right out of the oven slice of heaven can provide.

Aside from the historic appeal of old railroad cars, New Hope & Ivyland Railroad has nothing going for it. It is a very short run at a very slow speed for a very high price.  I hesitate to label it a tourist rip off for the unaware, but it comes close.    There are much better alternatives if your want a railroad experience.  If the train ride itself is your reason for going to New Hope, save the time and money and take the Light Rail from Trenton to Camden, or stops in between.  That is an actual passenger commute that rolls along the Delaware River for a while, and stations in some pleasant Jersey towns, like Burlington.  Last stop is the Camden Aquarium. If old railroads are your thing, make the day trip to Scranton, the old railroad capital of the USA. Plenty of museums and operational locomotives pulling plush Pullmans and a working roundhouse.   The NH & I experience will likely leave you feeling disenchanted.
Lotus Garden is no more. Drove by today and the sign was down and the shop was closed with a sign on the door.

Hua Kang Health Center is a first rate Chinese style massage spa sitting unexpectedly in the Marrazzo Shopping Center on Parkway Avenue in Ewing, NJ. It is bigger than most I have visited, with ten private rooms, each well appointed and very clean.    Their staff is well trained in traditional Chinese technique, plus Swedish and a little Shiatsu.  Lily, my masseuse, asked if I would like her to work deep tissue and walk on my back.  No problem.  She went from my shoulders to the soles of my feet like a dancer.  Very effective. With practically every step I felt/heard a snap, crackle and pop as she stretched me out.   Hot stones and steam towels alternated where I had the most discomfort, followed by her forearm and elbows probing the facets and pushing apart the disks in my spinal column.    It was an excellent, relaxing and therapeutic massage. I think I even fell asleep. At a buck a minute, it was a fair price.  After shoveling snow and feeling the sciatic stress, it was great to feel such prompt relief.    If they had a sauna or two, served fruit and hot tea, it would be just about perfect.

One of the nicer Asian markets in Philly proper, although there are very good H Marts out in the Northeast and Elkins Park.  The place is large, well lit, and stocked with all those things that have never been heard of by the Acmes and Giants of the world.  Need a regional chili sauce from Chongqing?  They have a variety of them.  Want thin noodles from Thailand?  Just ask for it.  Jonezing for sweet pea leaves for that special garlic recipe?  Yup.  It's there.  Need fresh fish for your father-in-law?  The red snapper is right off the boat.   The prices can be erratic, and sometimes the aisles are so overloaded with goods that two carts can't pass each other, but if that really bothers you, you probably never went to the markets in any town in Asia.  That's just the way it is.  Sell by dates important to you?  It may be better to just close your eyes.   Staff is very helpful and multilingual.  They even have a small apothecary to save you the trip to the herb shops in Chinatown.  Even had Wood Lock Oil.

The old Post office in Main Street, Yardley, PA, is the size of a large closet. It still has a wall of copper coated post office boxes, and sells stamps and packaging materials. It is really only a substation to the main US Postal Service facility on West Trenton Road in Morrisville.   It retains it's charm and historical ambience, despite the fact that services are limited and parking can be an issue out front of in back.   If you find yourself in the Borough of Yardley for a medical visit, breakfast of early happy hour, it is worth a few minutes of your time to stop in to enjoy the atmosphere and pick up a few sheets of forever commemorative stamps.   It will have you thinking of the way your grandparents saw the world.

What a terrific natural and historic resource Tyler State Park is! Looping trails traversing a hilly topography; good for hiking, biking, walking. Find the old homesteads in the park that reflect what this area looked like in 18th Century rural Pennsylvania, and occupied today by families renting them from Bucks County on long term leases.    Discover the beautifully rebuilt covered bridge over Neshaminy Creek, a great place for photos and dreams.  Rent a horse for a few hours.  Scramble up the foot trails along the narrow streams and get lost in time.  In July, find your own secret blackberry patch and pick your own, eating them and tasting their sweet essence.  Watch out for the thorns!    Rent a canoe and paddle upstream and out of sight of civilization.  Jump in the water and cool down.  Watch kids swing out over the flow from a rope tied to a high overhanging branch, and Geronimo into the water.  Walk along the creek bank and find an arrowhead among the river rock.    So much to do, so well utilized by we who know it.    Take a deep breath and appreciate the moment.

Nice Korean green grocery in the Morrisville Shopping Center on Old Trenton Road. Plenty to choose at prices better than the local supermarkets, but not as good as the true farmers' market at Tanners' Brothers in Richboro. Butcher and fishmonger, too.   Interesting oddities, too, like Polish kielbasa and German Milka chocolates.   Worth going to when a major veggie and fruit expedition is planned and you don't have time for Tanners' or the Bristol Amish Market.  Plenty to keep you curious, entertained and in the greens.

This DD franchise approximates the mean of all Dunkins.    Decent Java, but too dependent on the water quality.  Bakery goods sweet and addicting.   Biggest issue is the location in the Lalor Plaza down at the bottom of Lalor Street, just off Rt. 129.  No problem during the day, but a bit sketchy after dusk.  But, this strip houses one of my secret lunch houses, Perfetto Pizza; so I find myself in this hood at least once a month.    Big plus - Bilingual staff!

El Limon - Norristown is another in the locally born chain of solid Mexican restaurants that seem to be expanding almost monthly. It is a smallish shop compared to most of the others, but the quality of the kitchen is just as high.   I stopped in after an office meeting nearby. I found it decorated with colorful tables and carved back wood chairs depicting the beauty of the traditional town square with church steeples, red tile roofs and flowering bourganvillas. The Muzac was a bit too loud for dining, but surely the staff enjoyed it throughout the day.  My lunch of their tacos dorado (golden fried tacos) was very interesting and tasty. Stuffed within the rolled "flutes" were mashed potatoes, grilled chicken, and cheese. The softness just behind the crunch was fun and unexpected. On top was the mix of lettuce, tomato and fresh crema found on every plate. The red salsa in the table rocket liberally applied brought it all together. Liked it alot.   It was fairly priced @ $8.50, and filling enough to skip dinner tonight.   Norristown has many Latin American restaurants to choose from. El Limon (The Lemon) is worthy of consideration for your pesos.

Trenton Farmer's Market is an institution from the time there were actually working (and profitable) farms around Mercer and Bucks Counties.  It has seen better days, but is still a great way to get the basic foodstuffs of life all in one place, at reasonable prices, and avoid the corporatism that is the supermarket industry nowadays.    If that wasn't enough of a reason to do your consuming here when possible, there are several other good ones - butchers, bakers, veggie mongers, deli delighters, and even candlestick makers who produce first rate digestibles and other things that you would be happy to eat and serve your family and friends.    Yesterday I stopped in to pick up fruit, veggies, chicken, a little BBQ, and sticky sweets, to tide me over through the coming Nor'easter.  The shops that were open in the afternoon were happy to have a late customer relieve them of some of their stock.  I found some good deals.   While in the neighborhood you can visit other great places to purchase food or just enjoy a good meal.  Halo Farms, Rozmaryn, and Pho Tan are just a few of the Yelpworthy destinations to consider.

Old school Wawa in the center of Main Street, Yardley Boro. Small parking lot in front. Larger one in back, but you may not know its there unless your local. Small footprint that still manages to provide most of the products and services of the latest supersized versions.   I was there to pick up a chicken salad hoagie before moving on to my next appointment. It had been a while since ordering with their touch screens and found the shear number of pages I had to endure to be somewhat daunting. How many screens just for mayo?!   Still, the sandwich was good with fresh chicken salad, but perhaps less so for the torpedo roll. Enjoyable, nonetheless.   Everyone there was well trained and friendly from front door welcome to cashier thank you for coming. Price was very appealing, with the customized sammy ten inch coming in at under $7.   Little wonder why almost everyone wants a Wawa near their town.

If you are up and about very early, go to Cramer to get fresh donuts, muffins and scones.  Too, if you can order a cake for a special occasion, you will probably be quite satisfied. Otherwise, despite the charm of an old fashioned bakery, and the butternut aroma, the products are inconsistent, and pricey. The bread, bagels, rolls are not worth the trip. There are much stronger options for them only minutes away. To be a worthwhile destination everything must be good, available, and reasonably priced compared to the competition. Cramer is not quite all that.

This update is strictly for the breakfast this morning.  Their deli does prepare a limited breakfast menu, but unless you like microwaved eggs and sausage grilled between the cheeks of a pannini press, this might not be the place for you.  Absent a genuine grill they did a fairly good job on my sausage, egg and cheese sandy.  I do wonder if they clean that press before putting other breaded sandwiches inside.    While the taste and price were decent, I prefer the use of a grill to prepare my eggs and melt the cheese.  Although the coffee was okay and the ambiance very much "from the barn," I will likely not return for breakfast.   It remains a good place to buy farm fresh produce and enjoy the seasonal outdoor events.

The Pa Turnpike Commission has done a good job renovating the old service plazas along the roadway.  The Valley Forge stop is one of the smaller ones on the eastbound side.  It has only Starbucks and an A Plus Mini Mart for everything else.    It is clean and designed with high exposed beam ceilings and lots of glass to let in light.  Restrooms modern with waterless urinals and fast hand dry systems above the sinks.  It is certainly a big improvement over the old factory that was here.  But, it is still only a small oasis along a roadway that has had a difficult winter dealing with snow and vehicles trapped in bad conditions.    Hard to be a fan of something like a turnpike rest stop.  But, it is certainly A-OK.

Decent chicken salad sandwich, but the place is really dirty. Sat at a small table downstairs in their basement shop. The cracks in the red paint were black with grime and lack of strong cleanser for too long. Same for the floor and back shelves and undercounted storage space.   Need to do better and care more, even if never inspected by L & I.

Pat's Colonial Kitchen is exactly that - a first floor, cramped, cozy, warm, 18th Century breakfast and lunch place that suggests the way life was in 1813 in this community William Penn called his New Town.  If you enjoy living history, this is your place to chow down on pancakes, french toast, coffee, etc., for breakfast; and burgers, sandwiches, and salads for lunch, while imagining your horse and buggy are tied up to the hitching post outside.    Is it the best food you have ever had?  Some might say so, but that is only half the point of eating here.  Step into Pat's, and you step into real history.  The Revolutionary War was fought right outside on the street!  Geo. Washington really had his war council only one block away before deciding to cross the Delaware River and engage in the Battles of Trenton and Princeton.    Eat your breakfast and feel just as our forefathers did before we knew we had a country to call our own.   Judging by the far flung places the other reviewers call home, this is exactly what they came here for.
There are 89 other reviews under, "Yardley Inn Restaurant and Bar."  If you find yourself looking at only these two reviews, you are in the wrong place.

A few visits to Dr. Rosenman has satisfied me that he is a good physician with excellent human interactive skills.  Beyond the thorough examination from scalp to toes, he diagnoses quickly and all the while keeps a warm banter going to help keep me at ease.  The provides running commentary on what he is looking at, and while still in the examining room records his office notes on what he has observed and talked with me about, so I can understand more fully what he is thinking, and provide time for questions.    When he saw something that he was not definite about, he asked me to return in a month to allow him a second look for changes.  As a precautionary measure he took a tiny sample for biopsy.  Nothing to worry about.    The office itself is clean, if a little dated.  The staff appears to be all women, some busier than others.  Still, I was in and out promptly, and not required to wait more than 10 minutes before he saw me both times.  The payment desk is efficient, and the billings have been reasonable and understandable.    See you again in a few years, doc.  Thanks a lot.

Crash serendipity led me to DP Autobody after my M45 was rear ended last month on my way home from work.  Actually, the guy who hit me recommended I go there because his family knew them, and would give me (him) a better price.  I got three estimates, and I found that DP was the lowest. Too, the owner, Dave Miller, had a great personal touch with me as a customer, and I immediately had a sense of trust with him.    So we went through the insurance formalities and car rental nuisances, but in the end, when the car was returned to me, I had a brand new looking chariot.  The dings and scrapes were gone, and the paint job was impeccable.    I was so satisfied that I decided to have to car detailed there in a few weeks.  I will update the review after that.    It is so nice to have a totally satisfying experience when it comes to auto repairs.  DP is now my only autobody shop.

Viet Kitchen is operated by the same folks who had the earlier International Smokeless BBQ. The new place looks about the same. Now, they offer all day breakfast, pho and com dishes, as well as tabletop grilling for later in the day.   Our disappointment stemmed from the pho ga (chicken noodle soup). Although there was plenty of bird in the pot, the underlying broth was weak. It lacked body and flavor, and clearly had not been allowed to simmer and mature over time. Worse, about 20 minutes after first slurps, I began to feel symptoms of MSG poisoning. Difficulty breathing, heaviness in the chest and mild headache. Their attempt at a flavor shortcut was an utter fail.   The fried chicken (thigh and partial breast) was okay, but not worth the struggle with the pho.

Another of the Super Wawa gas station/convenience stores that seem to have sprung up almost overnight in this part of South Jersey.    The gasoline prices are competitive, but you never know who the real producer/distributor is for any of them.  So, it likely isn't wise to use it too often.  The convenience store takes its cues from the Sheetz, A Plus, Quik Cheks and turnpike service centers of the world. Every kind of sugar and quick energy drink is available.  In this case, the deli actually is capable to turning out decent sandwiches and soups.    I am not a fan of these places, but understand their efficacy.  They serve their purpose, and even offer reasonably good java.

This is a human-free parking garage.   It puts a premium on following instructions as there is no one around to answer questions most of the time.  Everything is completely automated, from drive in through drive out.  Similar to a car wash, your vehicle is driven onto a moving platform or track and from that point on, everything happens robotically. Your car is pushed left or right to align it with the entrance to the storage area.  It is then lifted off the ground much like a garage lift, and then transported inside the vertical parking structure until you return to pick it up.    It is critical to take everything you need with you, most importantly your keys.  Turn off the engine.  Use the same credit/debit card to extract your car as used upon entry. Go to the other side of the building for retrieval.  Failure to recall the proper card could result in a long wait until someone arrives to deal with this screw up.  Reading the other reviews it is easy to see how it would be very frustrating to have to wait.    The evening cost is $14 for the night if in after 5.  Not a bad deal.

Hiding in plain sight within the H Mart in Levittown is a small Korean restaurant, accessible to shoppers to eat in or take out.  They also do catering.  The primary orientation is Korean cuisine, but Chinese offerings are also available.    The menu takes the form of large format photos above the ordering window.  They are labeled bi-lingually.  The staff is friendly and conscientious.  The food is quite good.   Today, we ordered Mandoo Kook, a Korean Beef Soup loaded with Veggies, Rice Cake and Egg.  It came with Fried Dumplings and Pickled Relish and Cabbage on the side.  It was richly savory and complex.  Additionally, we had Jeyuk Dupbap.  As we all know, that is Spicy Marinated Pork on top of Steamed Rice, and a small Lettuce Salad.  Very enjoyable and filling.    While this corner of H Mart would never be mistaken for haute cuisine nor fashionable comfort, it does offer a richly sustainable meal and rock bottom prices.  Definitely worth arriving hungry and eating here before working the aisles for a full shopping experience.

Circle Deli is the nearest food outlet to my office, and we order take out for eating in from there a few times a week. They deliver timely sandwiches, soups, wraps, and a plentitude of snacks neatly packaged and with a smile.   I prefer to eat later in the day and have stopped off there occasionally to order my own custom lunch.  They are willing to make anything off menu that they have the ingredients for, and do it well.  They are super efficient and friendly as a hard working husband and wife team.    What is really amazing is how much stuff they can cram into a small space and not seem cluttered and claustrophobic.   Generally, I am not a deli lunch kind of guy, as I prefer to have a more relaxing meal than sitting at my desk.  But, at crunch time, Circle Deli is a convenient and worthy alternative.   I am a fan.

The soups and sandwiches are fresh and well made.   It is fun to watch the crew make a sandwich as they have a discipline/routine to it that is very zen, although they may not know it.  It is a very local place, and it helps to know Becky or her people to feel at home there. I can understand some of the pejorative reviews from new customers, because they are not known and the young workers are not always people persons.  Still, the product is good, and the prices reasonable.  Bottom line - I enjoy the walk from my office for a take out lunch on nice days, knowing I will return with a tasty sandwich along with the stroll through historic Newtown.  PS. Becky's Deli now has 2 outdoor tables on nice days.

East China Restaurant in the Giant Shopping Center in Morrisville, Pa., may have been in operation for a long time...and, it shows.    First impression upon entry is of a large buffet table (empty at night), torn carpet, dim lighting, and a desperate need of a makeover.  The temperature is lower than comfortable as demonstrated by the hostess/owner wearing her coat as she seats and serves.
